Then he arrives at the Nile in Memphis to Busiris, son of Poseidon, whom he kills along with his son Iphidamas and the herald Chalbes and the attendants at the altar of Zeus, where he used to murder strangers. Arriving at Thebes, he went through the mountains to outer Libya, in whose deserts he kills many of the wild beasts with his arrows. Having cleansed Libya, he went down to the outer sea, and taking a golden cup from Helios he crosses in it to the other side, sailing through the land and the sea and the ocean. Coming to Prometheus and being seen by him, he pities him as he supplicates and kills the eagle that was eating his liver, shooting it as it flew. In return for this, Prometheus advises him not to go for the apples, but to go to Atlas and bid him bring them, and to hold the sky himself in place of Atlas until he brings the apples from the Hesperides. Heracles, hearing this, goes to Atlas and bids him bring three apples from the Hesperides, explaining the labor. Atlas, placing the sky on Heracles' shoulders and going to the Hesperides, receiving the apples from them and coming to Heracles, says that he himself will carry the apples to Eurystheus, and bids him to hold the sky in his place. Heracles, having agreed, by a trick placed it back on Atlas; for Prometheus had told him, advising him to bid him take the sky until he made a coil for his head. Atlas, setting the apples on the ground, takes the sky, and Heracles, taking the apples, bidding farewell to Atlas, departs to Mycenae to Eurystheus and shows them to him. Thus Pherecydes in the second book (3 F 17 J.) relates.

c. That when Zeus married Hera, Earth brought forth the golden apples as gifts on the ocean, Pherecydes in the second book (3 F 16 b J.) says. A serpent, offspring of Typhon and Echidna, guarded them, having a hundred heads and voices of all kinds.

d. The Hesperides bustled: from appearing in the evening or from dwelling in Hesperia. The Hesperides were daughters of Phorcys and Ceto. 〈...〉 From one of them the island is named, which Geryon inhabited, having the dog Orthus, brother of Cerberus, whom Heracles killed; but others say they are daughters of Atlas.
1401. στύπος: trunk, stem. Lᴳ Gᴳ P
1404. χόλον: instead of χολήν (bile). Homer (Il. 16.203): 'with bile, then, your mother nourished you'. Lᵐ (P)

1405. μυῖαι πυθομένοισιν: πυθομένοις instead of σηπομένοις (rotting); whence also Pythia from the dragon having rotted there. (Or from those who come to the oracles in an inquiring manner; or from a certain Pythian child, whose name was Pythia, daughter of Delphus.) Lycus of Neapolis says that pus is also from this; for it is rotted blood.
